```{r setup, include=FALSE}

```

# Summary of the analysis

We model miles per gallon as a function of weight, quarter-mile time and transmission type, then check the usual regression assumptions.

# Data preparation

```{r prep}
dat <- mtcars
dat$am <- factor(dat$am, labels = c("automatic", "manual"))
dat <- dat[, c("mpg", "wt", "qsec", "am")]
```

```{r preview}
knitr::kable(head(dat, 6))
```

```

# Model fit

```{r fit}
fit <- lm(mpg ~ wt + qsec + am, data = dat)
summary(fit)
```

# Analysis of variance

```{r anova-table}
anova(fit)
```

# Residual plots

```{r diag-plots}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fitted(fit), resid(fit), xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
qqnorm(resid(fit))
qqline(resid(fit))
```

# Normality of residuals

```{r shapiro}
shapiro.test(resid(fit))
```

# Predictions

```{r pred}
new_cars <- data.frame(
  wt = c(2.5, 3.5),
  qsec = c(18, 18),
  am = factor(c("manual", "automatic"), levels = levels(dat$am))
)
knitr::kable(cbind(new_cars, predicted_mpg = round(predict(fit, new_cars), 1)))
```

# Conclusions

Weight is the dominant predictor, and the residuals look reasonably well behaved.

title: "Responder Rates in a Simulated Two-Arm Trial"
author: "Biostatistics Unit"
date: "2026-09-21"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

# Study design

The trial compares a new treatment with placebo. The outcome is whether a patient responds, and age is recorded as a covariate.

# Simulated trial data

```{r simulate}
set.seed(2025)
n <- 200
trial <- data.frame(
  arm = factor(rep(c("placebo", "treatment"), each = n / 2)),
  age = round(rnorm(n, 55, 9))
)
lp <- -1 + 0.03 * (trial$age - 55) + 0.9 * (trial$arm == "treatment")
trial$responder <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(lp))
```

The simulation has these features:

- Two arms of 100 patients each.
- Age drawn from a normal distribution centred on 55.
- A treatment effect that raises the log odds of response.

```

The response rate in each arm is the first thing to check.

# Response rates

```{r rates}
knitr::kable(aggregate(responder ~ arm, data = trial, FUN = mean), digits = 3)
```

# Age distribution

```{r age-hist}
hist(trial$age, main = "", xlab = "Age (years)")
```

# Logistic regression

```{r logit}
fit <- glm(responder ~ arm + age, data = trial, family = binomial)
summary(fit)
```

# Odds ratios

```{r odds}
knitr::kable(round(exp(coef(fit)), 2), col.names = "Odds ratio")
```

# Limitations

All data here are simulated, so the estimates describe the simulation and not a real treatment.

title: "Assay Dilution Series"
author: "Wet Lab 3"
date: 2026-08-20
format: html
execute:
  echo: false
---

## Aim

We want a calibration line that relates the assay signal to the concentration of the standard.

## Samples

Five dilutions of the standard were read in the plate reader.

```{r}
conc <- c(100, 50, 25, 12.5, 6.25)
signal <- c(2.10, 1.45, 0.88, 0.41, -0.05)
```

The lowest dilution came back slightly negative after blank subtraction.

## Log transform

The signal is modelled on the log scale, so we transform it first.

```

```{r}
log_signal <- log(signal)
```

## Fitted line

The last point is unusable on the log scale, so the line uses the first four dilutions.

```{r}
fit <- lm(log_signal[1:4] ~ log(conc[1:4]))
```

## Calibration plot

```{r}
plot(log(conc[1:4]), log_signal[1:4], pch = 19,
     xlab = "log concentration", ylab = "log signal")
abline(fit)
```

## Notes

Re-run the lowest dilution before the next plate.

# Purpose

Sometimes a draft redefines a familiar function to keep a report tidy. This page checks what a reader sees afterwards.

## Why Mask Functions

A masked function lives in the global workspace and wins over the one in base R.

## Defining the Masks

Four small replacements follow. Each one accepts anything and returns nothing visible.

```

```{r}
cat <- function(...) invisible(NULL)
head <- function(x, ...) invisible(x)
summary <- function(object, ...) invisible(object)
message <- function(...) invisible(NULL)
```

## Calling the Masks

```{r}
head(cars)
summary(cars)
message("working on the cars data")
cat("hello from the masked cat\n")
```

## Qualified Call

The `base::` prefix reaches past the mask.

```{r}
base::cat("Qualified call prints this line\n")
```

## Removing the Masks

```{r, echo=TRUE}
rm(cat, head, summary, message)
```

## Real Calls Again

```{r}
cat("The masks are gone\n")
```

## Wrap-up

Everything is back to normal.

print.report_card <- function(x, ...) invisible(x)

# Introduction

This report looks at how far a car travels before it comes to a stop, given the speed it was going. The data are the classic `cars` measurements from the 1920s, and the aim is a plain description a safety committee can read.

# Data

```{r}
summary(cars)
```

There are `r nrow(cars)` observations, one for each braking trial.

```{r}
plot(cars, xlab = "Speed (mph)", ylab = "Stopping distance (ft)", pch = 19)
```

Faster cars clearly need more room to stop.

```

# Model

A straight line is the natural first model, so we fit stopping distance as a function of speed.

```{r}
fit <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)
summary(fit)
```

# Diagnostics

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fit, which = 1:2)
```

The residuals fan out a little at high speed.

# Discussion

```{r}
cat("Each extra mph adds about", round(coef(fit)[["speed"]], 2), "feet of stopping distance.\n")
```

# Conclusions

Stopping distance grows quickly with speed, and drivers should leave more room at higher speeds.

# Transmission and weight

Manual gearboxes were more common in light cars in the 1970s. This note quantifies the link with a logistic regression.

## Question

Is a car's weight a useful predictor of whether it has a manual transmission?

## Raw counts

```{r}
boxplot(wt ~ am, data = mtcars, names = c("Automatic", "Manual"), ylab = "Weight (1000 lb)")
```

```

```{r}
table(mtcars$am)
```

## Logistic fit

The binary outcome calls for logistic regression; the code is displayed.

```{r}
#| echo: true
fit <- glm(am ~ wt, data = mtcars, family = binomial)
```

## Odds ratios

```{r}
round(exp(coef(fit)), 3)
```

## Predicted probabilities

```{r}
round(predict(fit, data.frame(wt = c(2.5, 3.5)), type = "response"), 2)
```

## Verdict

```{r}
cat("Lighter cars are far more likely to be manual.\n")
```

## Maunga Whau

The volcano grid holds elevations at ten-metre spacing.

## Grid

```{r}

```

## Heights

The elevations lie between the crater floor and the rim.

```{r}
range(volcano)
```

```{r}

## Contours

```{r}

```{r}

```

```{r}
